docs.title: Welcome
docs.text: This site will contain various crafts and methods that focus on minimizing the ecological, humanitarian and economical impact. It'll include materials you can collect from nature, somewhat easily scavenge from trash and things you can easily find in stores.

docs.title: 1. Synthetic Ochre (The Iron Acetate Route)
docs.text:
Yes, if you make iron acetate (dissolving steel wool in vinegar) and allow it to fully precipitate and dry out into rust powder, those particles are essentially molecular. They are incredibly fine—much smaller than anything you could ever grind by hand—and they will lodge beautifully into the grain of the wood.

However, there is a major catch if you are applying this to pine: If you plan to use the liquid iron acetate directly on the wood as a chemical stain (a process called ebonizing), it relies on reacting with the tannic acid inside the wood. Pine has very low tannin content. If you wipe iron acetate on pine, it won't turn a rich color; it will just look weakly gray and washed out.

To use it on pine, you either need to pre-treat the wood with strong black tea to add tannins, or you need to let the iron acetate completely evaporate into a dry synthetic rust powder, mix that powder with a binder, and apply it as a physical wash.

docs.title: 3. Grinding Bricks (The Best DIY Route)
docs.text:
Bricks are essentially baked clay, which makes them a fantastic source for red ochre (terracotta) pigment. The problem is that crushing bricks by hand in a mortar will leave you with a mix of fine powder and tiny, sand-like grit. If you rub that into wood, the grit will scratch the surface.

Grinding bricks also creates a massive amount of airborne silica dust, which is a nightmare to manage indoors.

To get around both the grit and the dust, you should use a process called Levigation.

docs.title: How to Levigate Brick Pigment
docs.text:
Levigation uses water to separate the microscopic pigment particles from the heavy, scratching grit. It also traps all the dust so you don't breathe it in.

1.Crush the Brick:Wear a mask for this step.

Break the brick into small pieces with a hammer, then grind it in your mortar as fine as you can stand to do it.

2.Mix with Water:

Dump all the ground brick into a tall glass jar and fill it with water. Stir it vigorously.

3.The 10-Second Settling:

Stop stirring and wait exactly 10 to 15 seconds. All the heavy, useless sand and grit will sink to the bottom, but the water will remain cloudy and colored.

4.Pour Off the Pigment:

Carefully pour the cloudy water into a second, clean jar, leaving the sandy sludge behind in the first jar.

5.Settle and Dry:

Let that second jar sit completely undisturbed for 24 hours. The microscopic pigment particles will slowly fall to the bottom. Carefully pour off the clear water, and let the remaining wet mud dry out.

Once that mud dries, you will have an ultra-fine, grit-free red pigment powder that is perfectly sized for staining wood grain!

docs.title: Using Soy Milk Binder
docs.text: Pre-wet your fabric and add it to your soy milk binder, completely submerged. Stir occasionally. Leave it there for 12-24 hours. Remove the fabric and squeeze out the extra liquid. Hang to dry until completely dried. Dip the fibre again in the soy binder until fully wet, then remove it, squeeze out liquid and let completely dry. Repeat the dip once more. Let the fabric set for at least a week, preferably more, before using any dye.

docs.title: Iron Acetate
docs.text: Iron acetate is a great mordant for fabrics and can be used to color wood.

docs.title: How to make
docs.text: Collect some rusty iron and put it in a non-metallic jar. Add vinegar, preferably enough to cover the iron. Put on a cloth over the opening of the jar and put a rubber band around it. Let sit for a few weeks.

docs.title: Important notes
docs.text: Do not seal the jar. The process creates pressure that needs to be able to come out.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text:
As a mordant. Saddener. Binds well.

As a Wood Stain.

docs.title: Soy Milk Binder
docs.text: Soy milk binder works as a great pre-treatment before dyeing natural fabrics.

docs.title: How to make
docs.text: Put in 1 gram of soy beans per deciliter of water. Let soak for 12 hours or more. Blend in a blender. Sieve through a cheese cloth or similar.

docs.title: Uses
docs.text: As a binder for Pre-Treating Fabrics For Dyeing.
